passage:
"Look at this," said Salma, pushing her phone across the sofa. "Professor Iyer wrote 'lol ok' under my draft. Is he laughing at me?"
Kiran read it twice. "Where's the rest?"
"That's all."
"Hmm. He put 'lol' when I sent him a late email too. He isn't laughing at me, he uses it to soften things."
"Really?"
"My sister types 'haha' at the end of every text, even when she's cross. It's like a cushion. And when my friend Nabeel writes 'lol' with no emoji, he's actually uncomfortable."
"So it isn't the letters."
"It's who sent it and how they usually write. Why not ask him?"
Salma sighed. "Fine. I'll reply with a question mark and a smile."

qa.q: What did Professor Iyer write under Salma's draft?
qa.a: Professor Iyer wrote 'lol ok' under Salma's draft.

qa.q: Why was Salma unsure about the message?
qa.a: Salma was worried the professor was laughing at the draft, since 'lol ok' can mean humour, politeness or discomfort. Kiran's examples show the same letters carry different feelings.

qa.q: What could Salma do to find out what the message meant?
qa.a: Ask the professor kindly, or compare it with how he usually writes, rather than reading the letters alone.
Kiran's sister types 'haha' at the end of every text, even when cross, as a cushion to soften the message.

grounding: Typed haha or lol can mean humour, politeness or discomfort, so tone and history matter more than the letters.

passage: I'm Sabina, and I used to think typing "haha" was just being funny. Then I noticed it was doing other work. When I told Bhupen his idea for the group project wasn't going to work, I wrote "haha, I don't think that fits 😅" so it wouldn't sound harsh. When my aunt sent me a long list of chores I typed "lol ok", and I wasn't laughing at all. Once Bhupen wrote "lol sure" after I cancelled our plan and I couldn't tell if he was fine or hurt, so I called him and heard the flatness in his voice. Now I look at the tone and the history before I decide what a laugh in text means.

qa.q: How did Sabina soften the message to Bhupen about the group project?
qa.a: Sabina wrote 'haha, I don't think that fits' with a sweating smile emoji so it wouldn't sound harsh.

qa.q: What was Sabina unsure about when Bhupen wrote 'lol sure'?
qa.a: Sabina wasn't sure whether Bhupen was fine or hurt after the cancelled plan, and the call let Sabina hear the flat voice. The typed words alone could not decide it.

qa.q: What could Sabina do when a laugh in text feels unclear?
qa.a: Check the tone and history, and call or ask in person if it matters.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt about the cancelled plan?
qa.a: Bhupen may have felt disappointed but tried to seem easygoing, which would explain why the 'lol sure' sounded flat.

grounding: Typing haha or lol can show amusement or soften a message, and tone and history matter more than the letters.
